analysis.one_liner: Gives freight train workers 72 hours off after working seven consecutive days.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, despite 202 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred railroads from requiring a train employee to go back to work after that employee had been on duty or on call every day for seven straight days, until the worker got at least 72 consecutive hours off. It applied to railroad carriers and their officers and agents. The goal was to limit fatigue among train crews, who are often on call around the clock. The bill was introduced in October 1999, referred to a House committee and then a subcommittee, and never received a hearing vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Train crews — engineers, conductors, and other on-board railroad employees — who would gain a guaranteed 72-hour rest break after seven consecutive days on duty or on call, reducing fatigue-related stress and safety risk. The public also benefits because tired train crews are a safety hazard to communities along rail lines.

how_it_helps.text: Bars a railroad and its officers and agents from requiring a train employee who has been on duty or available for duty every day for 7 consecutive days to return to duty until at least 72 consecutive hours have passed since the worker was released.

analysis.who_pays: Railroads would bear the scheduling and staffing costs of releasing crews for 72-hour rest periods, potentially needing more employees to cover the same traffic. Rail customers could face some of those costs passed through in shipping rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose new scheduling and staffing costs on railroads, which could require hiring additional crews and could raise freight shipping costs.
The protection only triggers after a full seven consecutive days on duty or on call, so workers in the first six days would get no additional relief under this provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For train crews and rail safety, the benefit is real: a guaranteed multi-day rest block after a full week on call addresses genuine fatigue. The costs fall on railroads' scheduling flexibility, and the bill is narrowly drawn — it does nothing for workers earlier in their week — so its practical reach is limited even had it passed.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Ground Transportation subcommittee from October 1999 until the Congress ended in January 2001, and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on October 18, 1999 by Rep. LaTourette.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day, October 19, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Ground Transportation, where it stayed.
The bill attracted 202 cosponsors — 164 Democrats and 38 Republicans — but no further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroads were better off because the bill died: they faced no new 72-hour rest requirement or the staffing costs that come with it, while train crews got no guaranteed rest protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Railroads, which faced no new rest rules

for.name: Rep. Steven C. LaTourette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through referral to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

for.name: 202 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; its Ground Transportation subcommittee held it without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was heavily bipartisan and Democratic-leaning: 202 cosponsors including 164 of the chamber's Democrats and 38 Republicans, yet it never advanced past subcommittee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have required railroads to release crews for 72 hours after seven straight days on duty or on call, adding scheduling and staffing costs. Its aim was reducing crew fatigue, which affects the safety of workers and communities along rail lines.
